title: Official scenarios to 2035 see gas dependence growing under current trends, and the planned alternative relies on a large renewable build-out and new gas infrastructure

rootCauses.cause: Demand keeps growing (peak demand up 5.5% a year in 2016-2022) while domestic hydrocarbon output declines. If nothing changes, the energy deficit, and with it imported gas for power, keeps widening.
The gas-based fleet inherited from past choices (FND-TG-100) means that new demand is met by gas unless renewable capacity is added at a rate far above the historical pace.

The strategy itself plans more gas infrastructure (Zarat field, LNG terminal, conventional capacity, Skhira combined cycles) alongside renewables. Gas would remain the largest primary energy source in 2035 even if the strategy succeeds.

dataGaps: The NDC 3.0 power-mix target. An unverified press report, Webmanager Center (19 May 2026, tier C), says it targets at least 50% solar and wind in the power mix by 2035. The author did not open that article. The UNFCCC registry file (https://unfccc.int/sites/default/files/2026-04/Document%20CDN3.0%20-version%20Finale.pdf) returned an empty HTML response to both curl and WebFetch, so the target is unverified and not used.

No projection of the electricity generation mix (share of gas in TWh or %) for 2030 or 2035 was found. The strategy synthesis gives only the primary-energy mix and renewable capacity targets. The full strategy report, STEG's generation expansion plan and the least-cost 10-year plan required under TEREG (DLR 8.1, SRC-TG-105) were not found online.
No official electricity demand forecast (TWh, peak MW) to 2030 or 2035 was found. Only historical peak growth (5.5% a year in 2016-2022, SRC-TG-105) is sourced.
No IEA or IRENA scenario specific to Tunisia's power mix was opened. The IEA country page returned HTTP 403.
How much gas the planned LNG terminal, the Zarat field and the ELMED interconnector would supply, or displace, in the power sector.
Whether the 2019 World Bank expectation of a gas shortage "starting in 2023" (SRC-TG-104) happened. Assessing this belongs to the energy-imports topic.

The 2030 renewable-share target of the updated strategy. The strategy synthesis cites only the earlier 2016 target of 30% of the electricity mix and states no 2030 share for the new strategy (SRC-TG-103). IRENA gives 30% (SRC-TG-106). The World Bank attributes 35% "in the energy mix" by 2030 to the updated strategy (SRC-TG-105). No primary text for 35% was found.
author: TahaGHZ

sections.heading: Problem
sections.content:
The official outlook to 2035 does not show Tunisia leaving gas behind. In the ministry's
business-as-usual scenario, natural gas rises from 56% of primary energy in 2021 to 59% in 2035, and
the energy deficit could reach 95% of demand if national resources and energy demand continue on the same current trend (SRC-TG-103). The strategy itself names electricity
generation, "dépendante depuis plusieurs années du gaz naturel", as the most vulnerable part of the
energy sector (SRC-TG-103). Even in the strategy scenario, gas would still be 44% of primary energy
in 2035, the largest single source (SRC-TG-103). Energy dependence would be between 33% and 76%
depending on how fast fossil resources are developed (SRC-TG-103). Getting there requires renewable
capacity to grow from 516 MW (end of 2023) to 4,800 MW in 2030 and 8,350 MW in 2035 (SRC-TG-105,
SRC-TG-103). That is about a 16-fold increase in 12 years.

This finding rests on primary-energy scenarios and capacity targets, not on a published projection
of the electricity mix. No such projection was found (see data_gaps).

sections.heading: Root causes
sections.content:
- **Demand growth on a gas fleet.** Peak demand grew 5.5% a year in 2016-2022 (SRC-TG-105). The appraisal estimates a 770 MW peak-hour shortage risk, about 16% of peak
  (SRC-TG-105). Peak demand reached a record 5,089 MW in January-September 2026 (SRC-TG-100). With a
  fleet that is over 90% gas (FND-TG-101), added demand is met by gas unless renewables grow faster.
- **Gap between targets and the pace achieved.** The 30% renewable-electricity target for 2030 was set
  in 2016 (SRC-TG-103, SRC-TG-106). The World Bank cites 35% for the updated strategy (SRC-TG-105). Renewables were 8.3% of production in January-September 2026
  (SRC-TG-100). The 2035 capacity target needs a build rate far above what has been achieved. The
  barriers are covered under the renewables topic.
- **Gas stays in the plan.** The strategy's investment list includes the Zarat gas field by 2030, an
  LNG terminal in 2027-2030, "les capacités conventionnelles de production électrique nécessaire",
  the Oued El Maleh pumped-storage plant and the link to Italy (SRC-TG-103). The World Bank in 2019
  described two new 500 MW combined-cycle plants at Skhira as "essential to provide grid stability"
  (SRC-TG-104). The strategy changes where the gas comes from (LNG, Zarat) and how much is needed. It
  does not remove gas from the power system.

sections.heading: Evidence
sections.content:
- Primary energy mix, oil products / gas / renewables: 2021 43/56/1; 2035 BaU 39/59/1; 2035 strategy
  38/44/18 (SRC-TG-103, figure 5).
- Deficit: 57% of demand in 2021 (excluding royalty), possibly 95% in 2035 "if national resources and energy demand continue with the same current trend" (no royalty qualifier stated for 2035)
  (SRC-TG-103). The World Bank gives 52% for 2023 (SRC-TG-105). The definitions may differ.
- Renewable targets: 8,530 MW (p. 12) and 8,350 MW (p. 17) for 2035 in the same strategy synthesis
  (SRC-TG-103); 8,350 MW and 4,800 MW for 2030 in SRC-TG-105. The Tunisian Solar Plan's earlier
  target was 3,815 MW in 2030 (SRC-TG-106).
- Renewable-share target for 2030: 30% of electricity was the 2016 target (SRC-TG-103, SRC-TG-106).
  The World Bank attributes 35% "in the energy mix" to the updated strategy (SRC-TG-105). The
  synthesis gives no figure for the updated strategy.

sections.heading: Why confidence is what it is
sections.content:
Low. The projection comes from one official scenario document available only as a synthesis
(SRC-TG-103), which gives no electricity-mix numbers. Some values were read from chart labels. Its
own 2035 renewable target is given twice with different numbers. The other forward-looking figures
are World Bank appraisal statements (SRC-TG-104, SRC-TG-105), not independent models. The direction
is consistent across sources: gas dependence persists or grows unless renewables and efficiency
deliver at an unprecedented rate. The size of the effect on the electricity mix is not sourced.

sections.heading: Links to other sectors
sections.content:
None found in the sources opened for the projection period. The current link to water pumping and
agricultural electricity use is described in FND-TG-101.

sections.heading: Leads for phase 2
sections.content:
- Stratégie énergétique de la Tunisie à l'horizon 2035 and its 2023-2025 action plan: https://energiemines.gov.tn/fileadmin/docs-u1/synth%C3%A8se_strat%C3%A9gie_2035.pdf
- Zarat gas field development, LNG import infrastructure (2027-2030), Oued El Maleh pumped storage (SRC-TG-103).
- ELMED Tunisia-Italy interconnector (SRC-TG-103, SRC-TG-105).
- World Bank TEREG programme (P507304), including STEG's least-cost 10-year generation and transmission plan (DLR 8.1): https://projects.worldbank.org/en/projects-operations/project-detail/P507304
- Skhira 1 and 2 combined-cycle plants (SRC-TG-104).
- Renewable concession, authorisation and self-generation regimes under Law 2015-12 (SRC-TG-105, SRC-TG-106).

sections.heading: Verification
sections.content: **Independent review, 21 November 2026:** pass after corrections. Originals checked: Strategie energetique 2035 synthesis (SRC-TG-103), p. 13 Figure 5 and section 3.2, p. 12 and p. 17 targets, p. 3 deficit sentence, and a search of the full text for model names (only ThreeME, for macro effects, appears); World Bank TEREG appraisal document, background paragraphs 5-6 and Challenge 3 (SRC-TG-105); World Bank Energy Sector Improvement Project PAD, pp. 9-10 (SRC-TG-104); IRENA RRA Tunisia 2021, pp. 1-2 (SRC-TG-106); ONEM Conjoncture energetique, September 2026, p. 34 (SRC-TG-100). Corrections made: the 770 MW indicator year changed from 2025 to "n/a (appraisal April 2025)" because the source gives no year for the estimate; the 95% deficit is now stated with the source's own condition (trend continuation) in the Problem and Evidence text; the unsupported clause "new generation investment lagged" removed from root cause 1. No reviewer objection was left unconfirmed. Independent teammate sign-off is outstanding; reviewer and author share the TahaGHZ identity, so the record is not validated.

Column layout of the tables quoted below, checked against the page images: "Réalisé 2025"
(full year 2025), then "A fin septembre" 2015 (a), 2025 (b), 2026 (c), then Var (c)/(b) and
TCAM (c)/(a). All "fin septembre" figures are cumulative January to September.

p. 33, table "PRODUCTION D'ELECTRICITE" (unit GWh), selected rows as printed [...]:

> STEG | 19510 | 11 561 | 15 163 | 15950 | 5% | 3%
> GAZ NATUREL | 19183 | 10272 | 14901 | 15755 | 6% | 4%
> FUEL + GASOIL | 18 | 874 | 18 | 60 | 234% | -22%
> IPP Solaire (3) | 81 | 0 | 54 | 478 | 792% | -
> AUTOPRODUCTEURS Solaire(1) (3) | 721 | 0 | 565 | 822 | 45% | -
> ACHAT TIERS | 221 | 65 | 162 | 162 | 0% | 9%
> PRODUCTION NATIONALE | 20533 | 14 067 | 15 944 | 17 412 | 9% | 2%
> Achat Sonelgaz (Algérie) & Gecol (Libye) | 2461 | 0 | 2045 | 2073 | 1% | -
> Disponible pour marché local (2) | 21810 | 14067 | 18010 | 19510 | 8% | 3%

English gloss: electricity production by source. In full-year 2025, STEG gas-fired output was
19,183 GWh out of 20,533 GWh national production, and 2,461 GWh were bought from Algeria
(Sonelgaz) and Libya (Gecol). The table has no row for a gas-fired independent producer.
Note: in the 2015 column the listed rows (STEG 11,561 + IPP 0 + autoproducers 0 + third-party
purchases 65) do not add up to the printed national total of 14,067 GWh; the table does not
explain the gap. Also, the full-year 2025 "Disponible" figure (21,810 GWh) does not equal
production + exchanges + purchases (20,533 + 26.5 + 2,461 = 23,020.5 GWh). The Jan-Sep columns
do add up (15,944 + 22 + 2,045 = 18,011; 17,412 + 25 + 2,073 = 19,510). The extract above
omits the rows HYDRAULIQUE, EOLIENNE, SOLAIRE (STEG sub-rows), Echanges (26.5 / -27 / 22 / 25)
and Ventes Gecol [...].

p. 33, text:

> Ainsi les achats d'électricité pricipalement de l'Algerie ont couvert 11% des besoins du marché local à fin septembre 2026.

English gloss: electricity purchases, mainly from Algeria, covered 11% of local market needs
from January to September 2026.

p. 34, text and chart "Mix de la production électrique à fin septembre 2026* (* y compris autoproduction)":

> La STEG conserve toujours la part du lion dans la production électrique avec 92% de la production nationale à fin septembre 2026. La production d'éléctricité à partir des énergies renouvelables s'est située à 8.3%.

> GAZ NATUREL 91,3% | FUEL + GASOIL 0,3% | ER* 8,3%

> La pointe de la demande d'électricité a enregistré une hausse de 5 %, atteignant 5 089 MW à fin septembre 2026, contre 4 837 MW à fin septembre 2025, établissant ainsi un nouveau record national.

> Par ailleurs, environ 543 MW de toitures photovoltaiques ont été installée à fin septembre 2026 dans le secteur residentiel et 150 MW sur la moyenne et la haute tension dans les secteurs industriel, tertiaire et agrigulture.

English gloss: STEG produced 92% of national output (Jan-Sep 2026); renewables 8.3%; the mix
including self-production was 91.3% natural gas, 0.3% fuel oil and diesel, 8.3% renewables.
Peak demand reached a record 5,089 MW. About 543 MW of residential rooftop PV and 150 MW on
medium and high voltage had been installed by the end of September 2026.

p. 34, methodological note:

> A partir de janvier 2023, la production des stations solaires dans le cadre du régime des autorisations est comptabilisée dans la production d'électricité « IPP solaire ». A partir de janvier 2024, la production de l'électricité à partir des ER dans le cadre du régime de l'autoproduction est comptabilisée. À partir de décembre 2025, la production des stations solaires dans le cadre du régime des concessions est comptabilisée dans la production des IPP solaires.

English gloss: solar plants under the authorisation regime are counted as "IPP solaire" from
January 2023. Renewable self-production is counted from January 2024. Solar plants under the
concession regime are counted as solar IPPs from December 2025.

p. 33, text:

> La production nationale d'électricité a enregistré, à fin septembre 2026, une hausse de 9% pour se situer à 17412 GWh (y compris autoproduction renouvelable) contre 15944 GWh à fin septembre 2025.

p. 6, text:

> Par ailleurs, la production d'électricité à partir des sources d'énergie renouvelables a progressé de 66%.

p. 29, text:

> D'ailleurs, la production d'électricité à partir du gaz naturel a enregsitré une hausse de 6% entre fin septembre 2025 et fin septembre 2026.

English gloss: national production rose 9% to 17,412 GWh, including renewable self-production
(Jan-Sep 2026 against Jan-Sep 2025). Renewable output rose 66% and gas-fired output rose 6%.

p. 28, text:

> Le secteur de la production électrique reste, de loin, le plus grand consommateur de gaz naturel (75% de la demande totale à fin septembre 2026), la production électrique est en effet basée sur le gaz naturel d'environ 91%.

English gloss: power generation is by far the largest gas consumer (75% of total gas demand,
Jan-Sep 2026); generation is about 91% based on natural gas.

p. 28, table "DEMANDE DE GAZ NATUREL" (unit ktep-pci):

> DEMANDE | 4 842 | 3 524 | 3 806 | 3 964 | 4% | 1%
> Production d'électricité | 3 542 | 2 581 | 2 815 | 2 968 | 5% | 1%

English gloss: total gas demand and the part used for power generation (full-year 2025:
3,542 of 4,842 ktep-pci).

p. 29, text:

> Nous avons noté une baisse de la part des cycles combinés dans la production éléctrique de 68% à 66% entre fin septembre 2025 et fin septembre 2026.

English gloss: the share of combined-cycle plants in power production fell from 68% to 66%
(Jan-Sep 2025 to Jan-Sep 2026).

p. 24, text and chart "Répartition de l'approvisionnement en gaz naturel":

> Les achats du gaz algérien ont enregistré une hausse de 4% entre fin septembre 2025 et fin septembre 2026, pour se situer à 2240 ktep-pci. L'approvisionnement national en gaz naturel a enregistré une hausse 4% entre fin septembre 2025 et fin septembre 2026 pour se situer à 3979 ktep-Pci.
> 1. Baisse de la part du gaz national de 23 % à 22%.
> 2. Baisse de la part de la redevance perçue en nature et cédée à la STEG de 21% à 22%.
> 3. Quasi-stabilité de la part des achats du gaz algérien autour de 56%.

English gloss: Algerian gas purchases 2,240 ktep-pci; total national gas supply 3,979 ktep-pci
(Jan-Sep 2026). Shares: domestic gas 22%, royalty gas taken in kind and passed to STEG 22%,
Algerian purchases 56%. The source says the royalty share "fell" from 21% to 22%; that is the
source's own wording.

p. 22, text:

> Baisse du forfait fiscal sur le transit de gaz d'origine algérienne de 17% à fin septembre 2026 par rapport à fin septembre 2025 en se situant à 531 ktep-pci. [...] A signaler qu'un dépassement des prélèvements STEG sur la redevance revenant à l'Etat Tunisien à fin septembre 2026 d'une quantité de 444 millions de Cm3, en cours de régularisation.

English gloss: the fiscal royalty on transit of Algerian gas fell 17% to 531 ktep-pci
(Jan-Sep 2026). STEG drew 444 million cubic metres more than the royalty owed to the State;
this is being regularised.

p. 21, table "RESSOURCES EN GAZ NATUREL" (unit ktep-pci; columns as above), selected rows [...]:

> PRODUCTION NATIONALE +F.FiSCAL | 1 926 | 1 915 | 1 501 | 1 390 | -7% | -3%
> Production nationale | 1 133 | 1 680 | 863 | 859 | -0,4% | -6%
> [...]
> Redevance totale (Forfait fiscal) (6) | 793 | 235 | 638 | 531 | -17% | 8%
> Achats | 2 824 | 1 668 | 2 157 | 2 240 | 4% | 3%
> (6) Enregistrement d'un dépassement des prélèvements STEG sur la redevance revenant à l'Etat Tunisien à fin septembre 2026 d'une quantité de 444 millions de Cm3, en cours de regularisation.

English gloss: gas resources in Jan-Sep 2026 were domestic production 859, royalty (fiscal
levy) 531 and purchases 2,240 ktep-pci. Footnote 6 repeats the 444 million m3 STEG overdraw. Our
arithmetic: 859 + 531 + 2,240 = 3,630 ktep-pci, against total supply of 3,979 on p. 24. That
leaves about 349 ktep-pci (8.8%) that the source does not explain. The royalty proper is about
13.3% of supply, not the 22% labelled on p. 24. The residual is plausibly the overdraw, but the
source gives no conversion factor from m3, so this is an inference.

p. 8, footnotes to the energy trade balance table:

> (5) Cession de gestion du contrat d'achat gaz de l'ETAP à la STEG à partir de juillet 2015
> (2) la redevance totale (redevance reçue en nature et cédée à la STEG + redevance reçue en espèce et retrocédée) est prise en considération dans la balance commerciale energétique comme importation à valeur nulle.

English gloss: management of the gas purchase contract moved from ETAP to STEG in July 2015.
The royalty (in kind and passed to STEG, or in cash and passed back) counts as a zero-value
import in the energy trade balance.

p. 36, chart "Répartition de la consommation par secteur pour les clients HT&MT à fin septembre 2026" and text:

> Industries 56% | Agriculture 9% | Pompages& ser. Sanitaires 12% | Tranpsort 3% | Tourisme 7% | Services 13%

> En revanche, d'autres secteurs ont connu une hausse des ventes, principalement le tourisme (+6%) et le pompage agricole (+5%).

English gloss: high and medium voltage consumption by sector, Jan-Sep 2026: industry 56%,
agriculture 9%, water pumping and sanitation services 12%. Agricultural pumping sales rose 5%.

p. 35, chart "Evolution de la pointe électrique mensuelle" (MW, January 2014 to September 2026). Labelled annual maxima, read from the rendered page image (added for FND-TG-220):

> 3465 | 3599 | 3400 | 4025 | 3916 | 4247 | 4030 | 4472 | 4677 | 4825 | 4888 | [2025 not labelled] | 5089

English gloss: labelled summer peaks for 2014 to 2024 and 2026, in MW. Each label sits on the
summer of its year on the chart axis (juil-14 ... juil-26). The 2025 maximum is not labelled.
SRC-TG-221 gives 4,837 MW for 2025.

p. 5, table "BILAN D'ENERGIE PRIMAIRE" (unit ktep-pci), read from the rendered page image (added for FND-TG-131):

> RESSOURCES | 3391 | 3982 | 2624 | 2549 | -3% | -4%
> DEMANDE | 9639 | 6841 | 7379 | 7881 | 7% | 1%
> Avec comptabilisation de la redevance(3) | -6248 | -2859 | -4755 | -5333
> Sans comptabilisation de la redevance (4) | -7041 | -3094 | -5393 | -5864

English gloss: in full-year 2025, primary resources were 3,391 ktep and demand 9,639 ktep. The
deficit was 6,248 ktep with the Algerian gas royalty counted as a resource, and 7,041 ktep
without it. The January-September deficit was 2,859 ktep in 2015 and 5,333 ktep in 2026, with
the royalty counted.

p. 7, text (added for FND-TG-131):

> En comptabilisant la redevance, le bilan d'énergie primaire fait apparaître à fin septembre 2026, un déficit de 5.3 Mtep enregistrant ainsi une hausse de 12% par rapport à fin septembre 2025. Le taux d'indépendance énergétique, qui représente le ratio des ressources d'énergie primaire par la consommation, s'est situé à 32% à fin septembre 2026 contre 36% à fin septembre 2025. Alors que, sans comptabilisation de la redevance, le taux d'indépendance énergétique se limiterait à 26% à fin septembre 2026 contre 27% à fin septembre 2025.

English gloss: the January-September 2026 deficit was 5.3 Mtep, up 12%. The energy independence
rate was 32% (36% a year earlier), and 26% (27%) without the royalty.

p. 30, table "Exploration et développement" and "Titres" (added for FND-TG-131 and FND-TG-132):

> Nb de permis octroyés | Réalisé 2025: 0 | A fin septembre 2025: 0 | A fin septembre 2026: 0
> Nb total des permis | 12 | 14 | 11
> Nb de forages explo. | 0 | 1 | 2
> Nb de découvertes | 0 | 0 | 0

> Le nombre total de permis en cours de validité à fin septembre 2026, est de 11 dont 10 permis de recherche et 1 permis de prospection

English gloss: no permits were granted and no discoveries made in 2025 or in January-September
2026. The table counts 0 exploration wells in full-year 2025, but 1 for January-September 2025:
the source contradicts itself. It counts 2 exploration wells for January-September 2026. Eleven permits were valid at end-September 2026: 10 research permits and 1 prospecting
permit.
resolvedSources.notes:
Monthly provisional data. The PDF has a text layer, but the text extraction scrambles the column
headers, so every table row above was checked against the rendered page image. The internal
figures do not fully agree. Generation is "about 91%" gas on p. 28 and 91.3% on p. 34. The
royalty share is 22% of supply on p. 24, but 531 of 3,979 ktep-pci is about 13%. The gap is
probably the 444 million m3 overdraw noted on p. 22, but the source does not say so. The mix on
p. 34 includes renewable self-production, which is counted from January 2024. Earlier series
excluded it, so shares before and after 2024 are not strictly comparable.

resolvedSources.title: Stratégie énergétique de la Tunisie à l'horizon 2035, Synthèse
resolvedSources.publisher: Ministère de l'Industrie, des Mines et de l'Energie, with UNDP (PNUD)
resolvedSources.extracts:
p. 7, Avant-propos:

> Par ailleurs, cette stratégie a été adoptée par le conseil des ministres organisé le 11 avril 2023.

English gloss: the strategy was adopted by the Council of Ministers on 11 April 2023.

p. 8, Introduction:

> En matière de sécurité d'approvisionnement, le secteur connaît une baisse continue de la production des hydrocarbures conjuguée à une croissance soutenue de la demande d'énergie. En 2021, le déficit énergétique structurel a atteint environ 57% (hors redevance) de la demande d'énergie. Ce déficit a tendance à s'accentuer et pourrait atteindre 95% de la demande en 2035 si les ressources nationales et la demande énergétique continuent avec la même tendance actuelle. En particulier la production d'électricité, dépendante depuis plusieurs années du gaz naturel, constitue la composante la plus vulnérable du secteur énergétique Tunisien.

English gloss: hydrocarbon production keeps falling while energy demand grows strongly. In 2021 the structural energy deficit was about 57% of demand (excluding the
royalty). If current trends continue it could reach 95% of demand in 2035. Electricity
generation, dependent on natural gas for years, is the most vulnerable part of the energy
sector.

p. 8:

> Il s'agissait de réduire la consommation d'énergie primaire de 30% à l'horizon 2030, par rapport au scénario tendanciel et atteindre une part des énergies renouvelables de 30% dans le mix électrique au même horizon. Ces objectifs ont fait partie intégrante de la stratégie énergétique de 2016 et la Contribution Déterminée au niveau National (CDN) de la Tunisie actualisée en 2021.

English gloss: the earlier targets were a 30% cut in primary energy use by 2030 against the
trend scenario and a 30% renewable share in the power mix by 2030. Both were part of the 2016
energy strategy and the NDC updated in 2021.

p. 12:

> L'objectif fixé par la stratégie est d'installer une capacité d'énergies renouvelables de 8530 MW d'ici 2035 pour la production d'électricité.

English gloss: the strategy's target is 8,530 MW of renewable generating capacity by 2035.

p. 13, Figure 5 "Mix d'énergie primaire selon les scénarios", values read from the chart
labels (Produits pétroliers / Gaz Naturel / ER):

> 2021: 43% / 56% / 1% | 2035 BaU: 39% / 59% / 1% | 2035 Stratégie: 38% / 44% / 18%

English gloss: primary energy mix. Natural gas was 56% in 2021. In 2035 it would be 59% under
business as usual and 44% under the strategy scenario, with renewables at 18%.

p. 13:

> Ainsi, selon le rythme de développement des ressources fossiles, le taux de dépendance énergétique serait entre 33% et 76% en 2035 selon le scénario de la stratégie à comparer à 57% en 2021.

English gloss: under the strategy scenario, energy dependence in 2035 would be between 33% and
76%, depending on how fast fossil resources are developed, against 57% in 2021.

p. 17, 4.3 "Les investissements requis":

> Développement du champ gazier de Zarat d'ici au plus tard 2030. [...] Construction d'une infrastructure de GNL au plus tard entre 2027 et 2030 pour assurer aussi bien l'approvisionnement qu'un stockage de sécurité. [...] Raccordement électrique avec l'Italie avant 2027. Réalisation de la STEP Oued El Maleh d'ici 2030. Installation des capacités conventionnelles de production électrique nécessaire. [...] Installation d'une capacité de 8350 MW en 2035 pour la production d'électricité renouvelable.

English gloss: planned investments include developing the Zarat gas field by 2030 at the latest,
an LNG infrastructure between 2027 and 2030, the power link with Italy before 2027, the Oued El
Maleh pumped-storage plant by 2030, the necessary conventional generating capacity, and
8,350 MW of renewable capacity in 2035.

p. 17, 4.3, same list (added for FND-TG-132):

> Relance de la prospection gazière et pétrolière avec un objectif indicatif de 30 puits d'ici 2035.

> Réhabilitation et extension de la STIR (50% de capacité additionnelle) avant 2030.

English gloss: relaunch oil and gas exploration, with an indicative target of 30 wells by 2035.
Rehabilitate and extend the STIR refinery (50% more capacity) before 2030.

p. 12, text before Figure 3 (added for FND-TG-292):

> L'Efficacité énergétique et la sobriété énergétique permettent la maîtrise de la demande finale dont l'intensité énergétique baisserait à un taux moyen d'environ 2,8% par an entre 2021 et 2035.

English gloss: under the strategy, final energy intensity would fall by about 2.8% a year on
average between 2021 and 2035.

p. 13, text before Figure 4 "Evolution de l'intensité d'énergie primaire selon les scénarios":

> L'intensité énergétique primaire devrait baisser à un rythme annuel moyen de 3.6%.

English gloss: primary energy intensity should fall by 3.6% a year on average (2021-2035). The
Figure 4 data labels (0.135, 0.147, 0.146, 0.143, 0.130, 0.103, 0.085) are not tied to years or
units in the text layer and are not used.

p. 17, "Energies renouvelables et efficacité énergétique":

> Développement de larges programmes d'efficacité énergétique dans les secteurs de l'industrie, bâtiment et transport.

p. 19, "Le renforcement de l'efficacité énergétique et des énergies renouvelables":

> Réviser le cadre réglementaire de l'efficacité énergétique et réformer le Fonds de Transition Energétique (FTE) afin de renforcer la politique de maîtrise de la demande d'énergie.

English gloss: the strategy calls for large efficiency programmes in industry, buildings and
transport, and a revision of the energy-efficiency regulatory framework and of the Energy
Transition Fund.
resolvedSources.notes:
This is a synthesis only. The full strategy and its modelling (scenarios, electricity demand,
generation mix in TWh) were not found online. The document gives two different renewable
targets for 2035: 8,530 MW on p. 12 and 8,350 MW on p. 17. SRC-TG-105 uses 8,350 MW. The
figure 5 values were read from the rendered chart labels. The chart shows primary energy, not
the electricity mix. The UNDP disclaimer on p. 4 says the views are those of the authors. Tier B
because it is a policy and scenario document, not statistics. Page numbers are printed page
numbers, which match the PDF.

resolvedSources.title: Tunisia Energy Sector Improvement Project (P168273), Project Appraisal Document
resolvedSources.extracts:
Printed p. 2 (PDF p. 11), para. 5:

> Natural gas and oil respectively account for 53 and 47 percent of Tunisia's primary energy demand in 2018. In terms of electricity generation, 83 percent derives from open and combined cycle gas turbines, 15 percent from dual fuel steam units (natural gas and heavy fuel oil) and 2 percent from renewables, mostly wind.

> More than half of natural gas, 72 percent of which is used for electricity production, is imported from Alegria; part of this is paid as gas transit fee. As a result, overall dependency on energy imports reached 51 percent in 2018 (compared to 7 percent in 2010) and will likely continue to increase in the future, reducing Tunisia's energy security. The dependence on a single source of gas supply makes Tunisia extremely vulnerable to supply interruptions.

Printed pp. 2-3 (PDF pp. 11-12), para. 5, continued:

> Projections anticipate a shortage of primary energy, particularly natural gas, starting in 2023.

English gloss: in 2018, 83% of generation came from open- and combined-cycle gas turbines, 15%
from dual-fuel steam units (gas and heavy fuel oil) and 2% from renewables. More than half of
the gas, 72% of which goes to power, comes from Algeria, partly as transit fee. Energy import
dependency was 51% in 2018 against 7% in 2010. Relying on one gas supplier makes Tunisia very
vulnerable. Projections expected a primary energy shortage, especially of gas, from 2023. The
document cites the ministry's Conjoncture Energétique for December 2018 for these figures.

Printed p. 3 (PDF p. 12), para. 7:

> STEG is responsible for electricity service throughout the value chain, for transmission and distribution of natural gas, and, since 2015, for gas imports from Algeria. In 1996, the generation segment was opened to independent power producers (IPPs), which can produce and sell electricity to STEG. Currently, 18 percent of electricity supply is provided by one IPP; 82 percent is generated by STEG and a small amount through industrial self-generation.

English gloss: STEG has handled gas imports from Algeria since 2015. Generation was opened to
IPPs in 1996. At the time of writing, one IPP supplied 18% of electricity and STEG 82%.

Printed p. 4 (PDF p. 13), para. 9:

> Fuel purchases and IPP payment account for more than 80 percent of the cost of electricity and are highly dependent on international oil price fluctuations, to which the gas import from Algeria is indexed, as well as exchange rate variations.

English gloss: fuel and IPP payments make up more than 80% of electricity cost. They follow
international oil prices, to which Algerian gas import prices are indexed, and exchange rates.

Printed p. 5 (PDF p. 14), para. 11:

> GoT plans to develop two new gas-fired combined cycle power plants (Skhira 1 and 2) of approximately 500 MW each, the first as a public-sector plant by 2022, and the second as an IPP in subsequent years. These plants are essential to provide grid stability as significant RE is integrated in the power system.

English gloss: the government planned two new gas-fired combined-cycle plants at Skhira, about
500 MW each, the first public by 2022 and the second as an IPP later, presented as needed for
grid stability as renewables are added.

Printed p. 10 (PDF p. 19):

> CPC is the only IPP in Tunisia's power market, owning and operating a 471 MW gas-fired power generation facility in Radès, which accounts for 19 percent of power supply in the country.

English gloss: Carthage Power Company (CPC), the only IPP, runs a 471 MW gas-fired plant at
Radès that supplies 19% of power.
resolvedSources.notes:
Donor appraisal document; it relies on ministry statistics. The CPC share is 18% in one
paragraph and 19% in another within the same document. Page references were taken from the
PDF text layer; printed page numbers come from the page footers.

resolvedSources.title: Tunisia Energy Reliability, Efficiency, and Governance Improvement Program (TEREG) (P507304), Program Appraisal Document, Report No. PADHP00156
resolvedSources.extracts:
Page 2, para. 5:

> Tunisia is facing a deep energy challenge due to its heavy reliance on fossil fuel imports to meet its energy needs, notably natural gas, which constitutes a large part of electricity production. The electricity mix relies primarily on natural gas (94.4 percent). [...] In 2023, Tunisia recorded an energy deficit of 52 percent of its primary energy needs, compared to 20 percent in 2012. Natural gas imports are responsible for close to 40 percent of the energy trade deficit.

English gloss: the electricity mix relies mainly on natural gas (94.4%, no year given). The
energy deficit was 52% of primary needs in 2023, against 20% in 2012. Gas imports cause close
to 40% of the energy trade deficit.

Page 2, para. 6:

> This strategy aims to achieve 35 percent of RE in the energy mix by 2030 with a target of 4,800 MW of RE capacity by 2030 and 8,350 MW by 2035, compared to 516 MW at the end of 2023.

English gloss: the 2022 updated strategy aims for 35% renewables "in the energy mix" by 2030,
4,800 MW of renewable capacity by 2030 and 8,350 MW by 2035, against 516 MW installed at the end
of 2023.

Page 2, para. 7:

> As of mid-2024, STEG accounts for 97 percent of the country's electricity production, with the remainder coming from the private RE sector, including rooftop solar projects. [...] By the end of 2023, Tunisia had an installed generation capacity of 5982 MW. [...] Tunisia's electricity grid is interconnected with Algeria and Libya, and electricity imports increased to cover 12 percent of electricity demand in 2023.

English gloss: in mid-2024 STEG produced 97% of electricity and the rest came from private
renewables. Installed capacity was 5,982 MW at the end of 2023. Electricity imports from the
Algerian and Libyan interconnections covered 12% of demand in 2023.

Page 2, para. 8:

> Despite the Government's efforts, the challenging financial situation of STEG as the main buyer has hindered scaling up private investment in RE.

English gloss: STEG's difficult finances as the main buyer have held back private investment in
renewables.

Page 3, para. 9 b) and c):

> The difference is due to especially high variable cost of electricity generation, estimated at US$0.11 per kWh in 2023, driven by Tunisia's reliance on expensive natural gas for over 95 percent of its power generation, most of which is imported from Algeria.

> Between 2016 and 2022, the peak electricity demand grew by 5.5 percent per year, while investments in new generation capacity were lagging. This has led to an increased risk of electricity shortages during peak hours, estimated at 770 MW (about 16 percent of peak demand).

English gloss: the variable generation cost was about US$0.11/kWh in 2023 because gas, mostly
imported from Algeria, supplies over 95% of generation. Peak demand grew 5.5% a year in
2016-2022 while generation investment lagged. The risk of peak-hour shortage is estimated at
770 MW, about 16% of peak demand.

Page 25, para. 76:

> The reliance on imported natural gas, partially indexed to Brent prices, exposes the country and STEG to cost risks from fluctuations in global energy prices and foreign exchange (FX) rates.

English gloss: imported gas, partly indexed to Brent, exposes Tunisia and STEG to world energy
price and exchange rate risk.

Page 36, DLI 8 verification protocol:

> DLR 8.1: STEG adopts a least-cost 10-year power generation and transmission investment plan consistent with the Tunisian Government's energy transition objectives and is approved by MIME. [...] DLR 8.1 verified for the year 2026 and DLR 8.2 verified for the year 2028

English gloss: a disbursement condition requires STEG to adopt a least-cost 10-year generation and
transmission investment plan, approved by the ministry, to be verified for 2026.

Page 3, para. 9 a) ii (added for FND-TG-221):

> High technical and commercial electricity losses. In 2023, total network losses stood at 18.4 percent, due to commercial losses (mainly fraud), under-spending on operation and maintenance (O&M), aging network assets, and lack of advanced metering infrastructure (AMI).

English gloss: total network losses were 18.4% in 2023, caused by commercial losses (mainly fraud),
under-spending on operation and maintenance, ageing assets, and no advanced metering.

Page 3, para. 9 c) (continued, added for FND-TG-220):

> c) Challenge #3: Deterioration of electricity supply reliability due to tight power generation reserve margin and lagging investments in electricity T&D networks . STEG financial situation has exacerbated implementation of its capacity expansion plan. [...] Furthermore, the financial difficulties of STEG have affected the reliability of the electricity supply and the implementation of the company's distribution investment plan. The impact of major climatic events such as the storm on January 24, 2019, and heavy rainfall in 2021 on the Quality of Service (QoS) is evident in the increased number of transient and permanent interruptions.

English gloss: STEG's financial difficulties have hurt supply reliability and delayed its
distribution investment plan. Storms (January 2019) and heavy rain (2021) increased interruptions.

Footnote 12 (page 20):

> In 2019 alone, storms led to over 5.6 million TND in damages and drove a sharp rise in energy not supplied (ENS) from 6.3 GWh in 2018 to 10 GWh. More recently, a nationwide blackout in 2023 underscored the grid's vulnerability to extreme climatic conditions.

English gloss: energy not supplied rose from 6.3 GWh (2018) to 10 GWh (2019) after storms. A
nationwide blackout occurred in 2023 (no date given).

Page 5, para. 16:

> PDO-Level Outcome Indicator 3 (Custom) / DLI 3: Reduction in the total electricity losses (technical and commercial) (percentage).

Results framework, DLI 3:

> DLR 3: Overall electricity losses (technical and commercial) have been reduced to 15 percent. (Percentage)

English gloss: the programme pays out against cutting total losses to 15%.

Page 2, para. 6 (added for FND-TG-191 and 192):

> Since 2010, the country has promoted energy efficiency and RE, notably through its solar rooftop program for the residential and commercial sectors, enabling the installation of 250 MW to date.

English gloss: the rooftop solar programme (residential and commercial) had installed 250 MW
by the time of writing (document dated April 2025).

Page 2, para. 7 (added for FND-TG-191 and 192):

> The RE capacity installed amounts to 516 MW, out of which 45 percent is owned by STEG and 55 percent by private investors. [...] In 2015, a regulatory framework was established to attract private investors through: (a) the concession regime for large independent power producer (IPP) projects; (b) the authorization regime for medium-size IPPs of up to 10MW for solar and 30MW for wind; and (c) self-generation by industrial firms, including corporate power purchase agreements (PPAs).

English gloss: installed renewable capacity was 516 MW (end 2023), 45% STEG-owned and 55%
private. The 2015 framework has three routes: concessions for large IPPs, authorisations for
IPPs up to 10 MW solar and 30 MW wind, and industrial self-generation including corporate PPAs.

Pages 2-3, para. 8 (added for FND-TG-191 and 192):

> Despite the Government's efforts, the challenging financial situation of STEG as the main buyer has hindered scaling up private investment in RE. [...] The process of developing new RE capacities owned and operated by the private sector has been relatively slow due to learning phase from initial experiences with renewable IPPs, increased costs following the COVID-19 pandemic, and a combination of bureaucratic inefficiencies and financial risks, but encouraging signs suggest that RE development is accelerating [...] In 2019, a 500 MW solar tender was launched of which 200 MW is under construction and 300 MW is nearing financial close. In 2022, a 1,700 MW tender (1,100 MW solar and 600 MW wind) was launched in three rounds, incorporating lessons learned from the 2019 tender. In December 2024, 500 MW of solar capacity was awarded for the first round, with competitive bids ranging from 3.1 to 3.3 USc per kWh, with the remaining capacity to be awarded over the next two years.

English gloss: STEG's weak finances as main buyer have held back private renewable investment.
Private capacity has come slowly because of a learning phase, post-COVID cost increases,
bureaucratic inefficiency and financial risk. Of the 2019 500 MW solar tender, 200 MW was under
construction and 300 MW near financial close (as of April 2025). The 2022 tender (1,100 MW solar,
600 MW wind) awarded 500 MW of solar in December 2024 at 3.1-3.3 US cents/kWh.

Page 24, para. 75 (added for FND-TG-192):

> However, risks exist in implementing the RE plan, which aims to significantly increase RE capacity from 516 MW at the end of 2023 to 3,300 MW by 2028, therefore impacting production costs and STEG's financial viability.

English gloss: the renewable plan aims to go from 516 MW at the end of 2023 to 3,300 MW by 2028;
the World Bank flags implementation risk.

Page 29, results table, DLI 1 (added for FND-TG-220):

> Baseline | Prior Results | Period 1 | Period 2 | Period 3 | Period 4
> 1:DLI1: Improved reliability of electricity supply (Minutes )
> 137 | | 135 | 133 | 130 | 128

Page 38, DLI 1 verification protocol:

> DLR 1: SAIDI is reduced from a baseline value of 137 in 2023 minutes to 128 minutes in 2028.

English gloss: SAIDI (average interruption minutes per customer per year) was 137 minutes in
2023. The programme path is 135, 133, 130 and then 128 minutes by 2028 (period 4 = Dec 2028).

Page 34, DLI 3 data protocol (added for FND-TG-221):

> STEG collects at the end of the year information about total injected power to the grid and amount of electricity sales. Total injected power should consider net generation of STEG's own power plants +imported power through interconnection + IPP's generation-auto consumption. The sales volume corresponds to the quantities of electricity sold plus the quantities recovered from fraud and prorated amounts. Losses in percent are calculated using the formula: [(electricity injected into the grid – volume of electricity sales)/total electricity injected]x100

Page 39, DLI 3 verification protocol:

> Losses in percent are calculated using the formula: [(Energy injected into the grid – volume of electricity sales) / total electricity injected] × 100where total injected power is (net generation of STEG's own power plants +purchased power through interconnection + IPP's generation-auto consumption), electricity sold is the total amount of electricity sales.

English gloss: the World Bank and STEG loss rate is (energy injected minus sales) divided by
energy injected. Energy injected is STEG net generation plus imports plus IPP output (minus
self-consumption). Sales include recovered fraud and pro-rata amounts. ONEM instead divides
network losses by gross production (SRC-TG-222).

Page 26, results framework, DLI 3 (added for FND-TG-221):

> DLI3: Reduction in the total electricity losses (technical and commercial) (Percentage) DLI
> Dec/2023 18.40 | Dec/2028 15

Page 29, results table, DLI 3 path:

> 18.40 | | 17 | 16 | 15.50 | 15

English gloss: the loss baseline is 18.4% (December 2023). The target is 15% by December 2028,
via 17%, 16% and 15.5%.
resolvedSources.notes:
The cover is marked "FOR OFFICIAL USE ONLY", but the document is publicly listed and
downloadable on the World Bank documents site (text version at the URL above, dated 4 April
2025). Page numbers are the "Page n" footers in the text version. The document gives two gas
shares: 94.4% (para. 5, no year) and "over 95 percent" (para. 9). The 35% target "in the energy
mix" by 2030 is attributed to the updated (2022) strategy by this document only. The strategy
synthesis (SRC-TG-103) mentions only the earlier 2016 target of 30% of the electricity mix and
states no 2030 share for the new strategy. IRENA (SRC-TG-106) gives 30%.
Its 8,350 MW for 2035 matches p. 17 of SRC-TG-103, not p. 12.

resolvedSources.title: Renewables Readiness Assessment, The Republic of Tunisia
resolvedSources.extracts:
p. 5, foreword:

> [...] with a 30/30 target to reduce primary energy demand by 30% in 2030 compared to the trend scenario; and renewable energy to 30% of the electricity production by 2030, in comparison to the installed 373 MW renewable energy in 2019.

English gloss: the "30/30" target is a 30% cut in primary energy demand against trend and 30%
renewables in electricity production by 2030. Installed renewables were 373 MW in 2019.

p. 23, 2.2:

> The monopoly on electricity generation, transmission and distribution from 1962 to 1996 was held by the Tunisian Company of Electricity and Gas (STEG – Société Tunisienne d'Electricité et du Gaz).

> Law No. 96-27 (April 1996) authorises the private generation of electricity through concessions provided by state authorities. It does not allow, however, unsolicited private power production (either from conventional or renewable sources). Only one concession agreement has been granted, authorising the creation and operation of Tunisia's first IPP (Carthage Power Company in Radès, 471 megawatts (MW)). This power station began operation in 2002 under a 20-year power purchase agreement (PPA).

English gloss: STEG held the generation, transmission and distribution monopoly from 1962 to 1996.
Law 96-27 (April 1996) allowed private generation by concession, but not unsolicited private
projects. Only one concession was granted, for the 471 MW Carthage Power Company plant at Radès,
which started in 2002 under a 20-year PPA.

p. 23:

> ANME, a public institution under the Ministry of Energy, Mines and the Energy Transition, became responsible as of 1985 for executing the government's policies for promoting energy efficiency measures and the deployment of renewable energy.

> Law No. 2015-12 sets the framework for renewable energy proliferation [...] Law No. 2015-12, however, was amended by Law 2019-47, dated 29 May 2019, with adjustments to allow for corporate PPAs.

English gloss: ANME has carried out energy efficiency and renewable energy policy since 1985.
Law 2015-12 set the renewable energy framework and was amended by Law 2019-47 (29 May 2019)
to allow corporate PPAs.

p. 41, Table 10:

> Decree No. 96-1125 of 20 June 1996 • Sets the conditions and procedures for granting the concession of electricity generation to private consumers

English gloss: Decree 96-1125 of 20 June 1996 sets the conditions and procedures for granting
electricity generation concessions.

p. 24, 2.3:

> By the end of 2018, total installed power generation capacity had reached 6 147 MW, of which STEG owns and operates 74.6% (4 587 MW). The remainder includes the natural gas combined-cycle IPP, commissioned in 2002 and managed by Carthage Power Company, with an installed capacity of 471 MW. Natural gas accounts for 94.5% of domestic installed power capacity.

p. 24, Table 2 "Composition of net power generation capacity, Tunisia, 2016 - 2018" (MW, 2016 / 2017 / 2018):

> Steam turbines 1 020 / 920 / 660 | Combined-cycle gas turbines 1 639 / 1 612 / 1 612 | Open-cycle gas turbines 1 772 / 2 004 / 2 004 | Hydro 62 / 62 / 66 | Wind 240 / 240 / 245 | Independent power producer 471 / 471 / 498

English gloss: at the end of 2018 installed capacity was 6,147 MW, 74.6% owned by STEG. Natural
gas plants were 94.5% of installed capacity. The STEG fleet was combined-cycle, open-cycle and
steam turbines, with small hydro and wind.

p. 24:

> In this context, domestic production of natural gas stood at approximately 2 139 ktoe, equivalent to 58% of the country's overall electricity production needs.

English gloss: domestic gas production, about 2,139 ktoe, equalled 58% of what power generation
needed (year implied 2018).

p. 32, Box 2 "Tunisian Solar Plan":

> Objective: 30% renewable energy in electricity production in 2030 [...] Target for installed renewable capacity: 3 815 megawatts (2030)

English gloss: the Tunisian Solar Plan targets 30% renewables in electricity production and
3,815 MW of renewable capacity by 2030.

Extracts below added for FND-TG-190 to 192 (renewables lane block 190-219).

p. 13, executive summary:

> The acquisition and implementation of grid transmission infrastructure by the Tunisian Company of Electricity and Gas (STEG) is subject to long-running public procurement procedures, resulting in a time lag between renewable energy plant completion dates and connection to the grid to send out the electricity produced.

> Private-sector developers have faced difficulties understanding the procedures to obtain authorisation for projects, given the considerable number of ministries and public institutions involved in renewable energy projects.

English gloss: STEG's grid investments go through long public procurement, so plants can be
finished before they can be connected. Developers struggle with authorisation procedures
involving many ministries and public bodies.

p. 23, 2.2:

> Law No. 2015-12, however, was amended by Law 2019-47, dated 29 May 2019, with adjustments to allow for corporate PPAs. This provides the right for companies adopting renewables for self-production to sell electricity to other consumers or companies with subscribed power greater than the threshold set by MEMTE electricity 30% and use the national grid network to transport electricity.

English gloss: Law 2019-47 of 29 May 2019 amended Law 2015-12 to allow corporate PPAs:
self-producers may sell to other consumers above a threshold and use the national grid.

p. 33, 3.2:

> Tunisia's total installed renewable power generating capacity had reached approximately 352 MW by the end of 2019, with wind energy at 245 MW, hydropower at 66 MW) and PV at 62 MW (IRENA, 2020b).

> Tunisia's wind generation development began in 2001, when STEG brought online a wind farm at the Sidi Daoud site in the northeast, with an initial capacity of 10 MW and later expanding to 55 MW in 2008.

> STEG launched two other wind farms in 2012 at the sites of Metline and Kchabta (Bizerte region). Together they account for a total of 143 wind turbines with a total capacity of 190 MW. The total electricity production of the three wind farms installed by STEG in 2017 reached 449 GWh, and peak production was recorded in 2014 at 507 GWh, as shown in Figure 17.

English gloss: renewable capacity was about 352 MW at the end of 2019 (wind 245, hydro 66,
PV 62). STEG's wind programme started with Sidi Daoud in 2001 (10 MW, 55 MW by 2008), followed
by Metline and Kchabta in 2012 (143 turbines, 190 MW). The three STEG wind farms produced
449 GWh in 2017; the peak was 507 GWh in 2014.

p. 36:

> Grid-connected solar PV systems are recent in Tunisia. Their installation started upon the issuance of Law No. 2009-7, which authorises self-production of electricity from renewable energy sources. Gridconnected solar PV has mainly been implemented through the Prosol électrique programme, initiated in May 2010 by ANME and STEG.

> By the end of 2019, 3 644 solar PV systems were connected to the LV grid. The total PV capacity installed is evaluated at around 11 298 kWp, 90% of which were installed in the residential sector.

English gloss: grid-connected PV began after Law 2009-7 allowed renewable self-production,
mainly through Prosol Elec, started in May 2010 by ANME and STEG. The report gives 3,644 LV
systems and about 11.3 MWp at the end of 2019.

p. 46, 4.2:

> Following lengthy discussions regarding the guaranteed purchase tariffs and the modalities of their application and revision, however, the decision was taken to grant authorisations only based on calls for projects announced by MIEM and within the limits of the objectives set by the annual notice.

English gloss: after long debate on guaranteed tariffs, authorisations were granted only through
ministry calls for projects within an annual quota, instead of a posted feed-in tariff.

p. 48:

> MIEM launched pre-qualification tenders on 23 May 2018 for the realisation by concession (build, own, operate) of five solar PV plants, totalling a capacity of 500 MW, and four wind farms with a total capacity of 500 MW.

p. 49:

> Despite the delay in the bidding process, five bids were received for the 500 MW solar tender. The proposed bids were all within the range of USD 0.0244/kWh to USD 0.0286/kWh (MEMTE, 2019a).

> For renewable projects under the Authorisation scheme, MISME proceeded in May 2017 to launch the first call for projects for the development of 210 MW from solar PV and wind.

English gloss: concession pre-qualification for 500 MW PV and 500 MW wind was launched on 23 May
2018. Five bids were received for the 500 MW solar tender, at 2.44-2.86 US cents/kWh. The first
authorisation call (May 2017) was for 210 MW of PV and wind.

p. 52:

> The preparatory phase of this programme did not include all the relevant stakeholders and did not consider the various aspects relating to the implementation of energy planning, such as access to land.

p. 54-55:

> With respect to the Authorisation scheme, one of the main concerns for private developers is the absence of standardised contractual documents for bid submissions, thus resulting in discrepancies and lack of transparency, eventually reducing the bankability of PPAs. In general, the absence of any guarantee scheme regarding the off-taker risks limits the attractiveness of PPAs.
> The results of the first call for projects of May 2017 highlighted the constraints in project bankability, where most private sector offers were conditional upon the change in the structure of the PPA.
> Owing to this problem, no wind project has been selected at this round of call for projects.

English gloss: the 2017-2022 programme was planned without all stakeholders and ignored issues
such as land access. Developers lacked standard bid documents, and there was no guarantee
against off-taker (STEG) risk, which reduced PPA bankability. Most offers in the May 2017 call
were conditional on changing the PPA, and no wind project was selected in that round.

p. 28, text and Table 7 (added for FND-TG-290):

> In addition to the above tariffs, there were natural gas tariffs for grey cement industries. These related to high pressure and medium pressure lines (Table 7).

> Table 7. Medium-voltage tariffs for grey cement industry, Tunis — High pressure | ≥ 41 868 | 105.99 | 0.06 | 1 xPg | 0.020 ; Medium pressure | 4 187 – 125 604 | 7.1 | 0.21 | 1.032 xPg | 0.020 ; Note: [...] Pg=purchase of natural gas [...] * Price of energy based on the purchase price of natural gas of 0.005 (USD/MJ).

English gloss: grey cement plants have their own natural gas tariff, whose energy price is
indexed to the purchase price of natural gas (Pg): 1 x Pg on high pressure and 1.032 x Pg on
medium pressure. The table is mistitled "medium-voltage tariffs" but lists gas tariffs (columns:
subscribed flow MJ/h, subscription fee, price of energy, indexation formula, energy price).
resolvedSources.notes:
Prepared with ANME and the ministry. Some capacity data come from interviews with ANME and
STEG. The table's totals (5,260 / 5,315 / 6,147 MW) do not equal the sum of the listed rows for
2018. The 2018 rows (STEG 4,587 + rooftop 62 + IPP 498) sum to 5,147 MW. The gas units (steam
660 + combined cycle 1,612 + open cycle 2,004 + IPP 498) sum to 4,774 MW, about 93%, not the
94.5% stated in the text. This is our arithmetic; the report does not explain the gap. Page numbers are printed page numbers, which match the PDF.

relatedItems.title: Tunisia locked its power system into gas in the 1990s and 2000s, when Algerian transit royalty gas and new domestic fields gave it a gas supply base
Over 90% of Tunisian electricity comes from natural gas, and 78% of Tunisia's gas supply is not domestic (mainly Algerian purchases plus royalty gas)
